unit.title: Funds and ETFs
unit.description: Funds, ETFs, fees, index investing and how to read their factsheet

steps.title: Pooled investing
steps.body:
An **investment fund** pools money from thousands of people, and a **management company** invests it according to a policy («European shares», «short-term fixed income»…).

You buy **units**. Their price, the **net asset value (NAV)**, is calculated once a day.

steps.title: Who's who
steps.body:
• **Management company:** decides what to buy.
• **Custodian:** holds the assets and keeps an eye on the management company.
• **CNMV:** registers and supervises Spanish funds.

The fund's money **belongs to the unitholders** and is kept separate from the management company's: if the management company goes bust, it can't take it with it.

steps.title: The big advantage in Spain
steps.body: You can **transfer** from one fund to another **without paying tax** until you sell out completely. There are **actively managed** funds (the manager picks investments to try to beat the index) and **index** funds (they copy an index at low cost).
steps.key: A fund pools many people's money to buy many assets, with a management company in charge.
steps.tip: Transferring between funds is like changing lanes without paying a toll.

steps.title: A fund that trades on the market
steps.body:
An **ETF** (*Exchange Traded Fund*) is a fund that **trades on the stock exchange** like a share: you buy and sell it at any time during trading hours, at that moment's price.

It almost always **copies an index** (S&P 500, MSCI World, bonds, gold…) at very low cost: from **0.03 % to 0.30 %** a year for the big ones.

steps.title: ETF or traditional fund
steps.body:
• **Price:** the ETF, at every moment; the fund, once a day.
• **Where:** the ETF, through a broker; the fund, through the management company, a bank or a platform.
• **Tax in Spain:** the ETF is taxed on every sale; the fund allows **transfers** without paying tax.
• **Extra ETF costs:** broker's commission and *spread*.

steps.title: UCITS ETFs
steps.body: A retail investor in the EU buys European **UCITS** ETFs, which come with a **KID**. Many US ETFs can't be sold to European retail investors because they don't have a KID.
steps.key: An ETF is a fund, almost always an index one, that you buy and sell on the stock exchange like a share.
steps.tip: An index ETF is like buying the whole supermarket instead of a single product.

u10l3.title: Fees: the TER and hidden costs

steps.title: The TER
steps.body:
The **TER** or **ongoing charges** is what a fund or ETF charges you every year to manage it. You never get a bill: it's taken little by little out of the fund's value.

An index fund might charge 0.1–0.3 %; many active funds in Spain, 1.5 % or more.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Put €10,000 in for 30 years at 7 % and compare a 0.2 % cost with a 1.5 % one: the difference is over €22,000.
steps.tip: These are examples, not promises: the stock market doesn't return 7 % every year.

steps.title: Hidden costs
steps.body: On top of the TER: the broker's commission per trade, *spread*, custody fees, currency exchange and, for some funds, entry or exit fees. Add them all up.
steps.key: Every 1 % a year in costs eats a huge chunk of the result, because of compound interest.
steps.tip: 1.5 % a year sounds like nothing. Over 30 years, it's a third of your money.

steps.title: What the data says (SPIVA)
steps.body:
Every six months S&P Dow Jones Indices compares active funds with their index in the **SPIVA** report. In Europe, at the end of 2025:

• Over **1 year**, **81.8 %** of European equity funds lagged their index.
• Over **10 years**, **97 %**.

And of the few that win over one period, hardly any do it again.

steps.title: Sharpe's arithmetic
steps.body:
1. All investors together **are** the market.
2. Before costs, the average active investor earns the same as the market.
3. After costs, they **must** earn less.

It's not that managers are bad: they compete against each other and charge more.

steps.title: What it means for you
steps.body: Picking today the active fund that will beat the index over the next 15 years is very hard: last year's top performer rarely repeats. That's why many people choose index investing. Buffett won a 10-year bet with an S&P 500 index fund against a selection of *hedge funds*.
steps.key: Over the long run, the vast majority of active funds return less than their index, mainly because of costs.
steps.tip: If hardly anyone beats the index, buying the index already puts you ahead of almost everyone.

steps.title: Two versions of the same fund
steps.body:
• **Accumulating (Acc):** the dividends the fund receives are **reinvested** inside it. You get nothing paid out; your units are worth more.
• **Distributing (Dist):** the fund **pays** you the dividends, usually every quarter or every six months.

The portfolio of companies is the same.

steps.title: Tax in Spain
steps.body:
What a distributing fund pays out **is taxed that year** (with 19 % withheld). With an accumulating fund **you pay nothing until you sell**: that money keeps compounding.

Example: €10,000 with a 3 % dividend yield. Distributing: €300 gross, €243 net. Accumulating: the €300 keep working.

steps.title: Which suits each stage
steps.body: To **build up** wealth over years, the accumulating version is usually more efficient. The distributing one makes sense if you **need income** (in retirement, for example). It's not that one returns more: what changes is when you pay tax.
steps.key: Accumulating reinvests and defers tax; distributing pays you income that's taxed every year.
steps.tip: Look at the ETF's name: «Acc» or «Dist» tells you which it is.

steps.title: Physical replication
steps.body:
The ETF **buys the shares** in the index.

• **Full:** all of them, at their exact weight.
• **Sampling** (optimised): a representative selection, useful for indices with thousands of stocks.

Many lend out some of their shares in exchange for a fee (**securities lending**), backed by collateral.

steps.title: Synthetic replication
steps.body:
The ETF holds a different basket of assets and signs a **swap** with a bank (the **counterparty**), which pays it the index's return.

Advantage: it can track the index very precisely and, in some cases, save on tax. Risk: the counterparty failing. The UCITS rules cap that exposure at **10 %** of the fund.

steps.title: How far it strays
steps.body: **Tracking difference** is how far the ETF falls behind (or gets ahead of) its index over a year. It's usually similar to the TER. Look at it alongside the ETF's size and its replication method.
steps.key: Physical: it buys what's in the index. Synthetic: a bank pays it what the index does.
steps.tip: Neither kind of replication is bad: what matters is understanding the risk each one adds.

steps.title: Three mandatory pages
steps.body:
Every fund or ETF sold to retail investors in the EU has a **KID** (Key Information Document): **3 pages** at most, always with the same sections:

• What the product is and its objective.
• What risks you run and what you could get back.
• What happens if the provider can't pay.
• What the **costs** are.
• How long you should hold it.
• How to complain.

steps.title: The risk indicator
steps.body:
It's a scale from **1** (lowest risk) to **7** (highest). A money market fund is usually a 1; a global equity fund, around 4; a single-sector or emerging-markets fund, higher.

You'll also see performance **scenarios** (stress, unfavourable, moderate, favourable): they're simulations, not promises.

steps.title: What to look for in a minute
steps.body:
1. **ISIN:** the fund's ID card (12 characters; it starts with the country, like IE or LU).
2. **Objective and policy:** what does it buy?
3. **Risk indicator** (1–7).
4. Annual **costs**.
5. **Recommended holding period.**
steps.key: In 3 pages, the KID tells you what you're buying, how much it can hurt and what it costs.
steps.tip: If you don't understand a product's KID, don't buy it.

u10l1-1.prompt: Match each player to its role.
u10l1-1.explanation: Each player keeps an eye on another: that's how unitholders' money is protected from the management company.
right: Holds the assets and keeps watch

u10l1-2.prompt: A fund has a net asset value of €12.50. You invest €1,000. How many units do you buy?

u10l1-3.prompt: A year later the net asset value is €13.75. How much are your 80 units worth?

u10l1-4.prompt: If the fund's management company goes bust, what happens to your money?
options: It's lost along with the management company
It's covered by the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (deposit guarantee scheme)
It still belongs to the unitholders: the fund's assets are kept separate
u10l1-4.explanation: The fund's assets don't belong to the management company. Careful: Spain's deposit guarantee scheme (FGD) covers deposits, not investment funds.

u10l1-5.prompt: A traditional fund's net asset value changes every second, like a share.
u10l1-5.explanation: It's calculated once a day. The one that trades throughout the session is the ETF.

u10l1-6.prompt: In Spain you can move money from one fund to another without paying tax if you do it by transfer.
u10l1-6.explanation: You only pay when you finally cash out.

options: Usually charges more than 1 % a year
Changes the portfolio based on the manager's view
The manager picks companies to beat the index
u10l1-7.explanation: Active management tries to beat the index and charges more for it; index investing copies it cheaply.

u10l1-8.prompt: Pablo has €5,000 in a fund with a €1,000 gain and wants to switch to a cheaper fund. How does he do it?
options: He sells, gets the money in his account and buys the new one
He requests a transfer from the old fund to the new one
u10l1-8.explanation: A transfer lets you switch funds without going through Hacienda (the Spanish tax authority), as long as the money doesn't pass through your account.
feedback: When he sells, he's taxed on the €1,000 gain (about €190) before reinvesting.
You can, and in Spain with a tax advantage.
Good: the money moves directly without being taxed; he'll pay when he cashes out completely.

u10l1-9.prompt: The price of one unit of a fund is called its ____ value.
u10l1-9.explanation: It's the fund's assets divided by its number of units, calculated every day.

u10l1-10.prompt: What advantages does a fund have over buying individual shares? Select all.
options: In Spain it can be transferred without paying tax
u10l1-10.explanation: A normal investment fund doesn't guarantee gains: its value goes up and down with what it holds.

u10l2-1.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u10l2-1.explanation: These are the four words you'll see when you look up any ETF.
right: Basket of companies the ETF copies
Fund that trades on the stock exchange

options: You pay a broker's commission and spread
You can sell it at any time during the session
Can be transferred without paying tax in Spain
You buy it at 11:37 at the price you see on screen
Its price is calculated once a day
u10l2-2.explanation: Trading on the exchange gives the ETF flexibility; the transfer regime is the fund's big advantage in Spain.

u10l2-3.prompt: This chart is an index that several ETFs copy: an ETF tracking it will do the same, minus its costs. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u10l2-3.explanation: An index ETF doesn't remove the market's ups and downs: you get exactly what the index does, for better and for worse.

u10l2-4.prompt: What annual cost do the big index ETFs usually have?
u10l2-4.explanation: Copying an index is cheap: you don't need a team picking companies.

u10l2-5.prompt: In Spain, if you sell an ETF to buy another one on the same day, you don't pay tax.
u10l2-5.explanation: ETFs don't have the transfer regime: every sale at a gain is taxed.

u10l2-6.prompt: Why can't a European retail investor buy many US ETFs?
options: Because investing in dollars is banned
Because they don't have a KID
u10l2-6.explanation: Without a KID, they can't be marketed to retail investors in the EU.

u10l2-7.prompt: You buy 15 units of an ETF at €98.40 and the broker charges a €2 commission. How much do you pay in total?

u10l2-8.prompt: An ETF can be bought and sold throughout the trading session.
u10l2-8.explanation: It trades like a share, with a price that changes all the time.

options: It has no risk at all
You buy it like a share, but inside there's a basket of lots of companies
u10l2-9.explanation: You buy it the way you'd buy a share; the risk is that of the whole basket.
feedback: It carries the risk of the index it copies: if the market falls 30 %, so does the ETF.
That's it! An MSCI World one holds over a thousand companies from developed countries.
You buy it like a share, but inside it holds hundreds or thousands of companies.
lines: I've been told an ETF is «like a share».
So is it just as risky as buying a single company?

u10l2-10.prompt: The ETFs a retail investor can buy in the EU usually carry the ____ label.
u10l2-10.explanation: It's the European framework that sets rules on diversification, custody and disclosure.

u10l3-1.prompt: €10,000 over 30 years at 7 % a year with no costs grows to €76,123. With 1 % in annual costs (6 % net), how much? (round to the nearest euro)

u10l3-2.prompt: With those figures, how much does that 1 % a year cost you in total over 30 years? (round)
u10l3-2.explanation: 76,123 − 57,435 = €18,688: almost twice what you invested, just in costs.

u10l3-3.prompt: You have €20,000 in a fund with a TER of 1.8 %. How much do you pay this year?
u10l3-3.explanation: 20,000 × 1.8 % = €360. In an index fund at 0.2 % it would be €40.

u10l3-4.prompt: Where do you find a fund's ongoing charges?
options: On a monthly bill from the management company
u10l3-4.explanation: They're required to appear in the KID, along with the other costs.

u10l3-5.prompt: Which costs can reduce your return? Select all.
options: The fund having lots of unitholders
u10l3-5.explanation: So can the spread, custody fees and tax. The number of unitholders isn't a cost.

u10l3-6.prompt: Ana's bank offers her an equity fund with a 2 % TER «because it's run by a star team». A similar index fund charges 0.2 %. What does she think?
options: She picks the one with the nicer logo
That the expensive one has to earn 1.8 points more every year just to break even
If it's a star team, it's worth it
u10l3-6.explanation: A high cost is a guaranteed handicap; the supposed skill to make up for it isn't.
feedback: The logo doesn't change the maths: what you pay each year does.
Good: the cost is certain; beating the index isn't.
To make up for it, the team has to beat the index by 1.8 points a year for years. Very few manage it.

u10l3-7.prompt: Order from highest to lowest result: €10,000 over 30 years with the market at 7 %.

u10l3-8.prompt: A 1.5 % TER only takes 1.5 % off your final result after 30 years.
u10l3-8.explanation: It's charged every year and compounds: over 30 years it takes about a third of the result.

u10l3-9.prompt: The annual cost of a fund or ETF is called ongoing charges or the ____.
u10l3-9.explanation: Total Expense Ratio. You'll find it in the KID.

options: It's taken out of the fund's value every day, which is why you don't see it
Hacienda (the tax authority) collects it at the end of the year
u10l3-10.explanation: Not seeing a charge doesn't mean you're not paying: the TER has already been taken out of the net asset value.
feedback: That's it! It's the quietest cost: no bill arrives, but you pay it.
It isn't a tax: it's what the management company keeps.
It does: it comes out of the fund's value every day, which is why you don't see it.
lines: My fund charges 1.8 %, but nothing has ever been taken from my account 🤔

u10l4-1.prompt: According to SPIVA (Europe, end of 2025), what percentage of European equity funds lagged their index over 10 years?
u10l4-1.explanation: Over 1 year it was already 81.8 %; over 10 years, almost all of them.

u10l4-2.prompt: Out of 100 active European equity funds, how many beat their index over 10 years, going by that 97 %?
u10l4-2.explanation: 100 − 97 = 3. And the real problem is finding those 3 in advance.

u10l4-3.prompt: Put William Sharpe's reasoning in order.
options: Before costs, the average active investor earns the same as the market
The active investor pays more fees and trades more
After costs, the average active investor earns less
All investors together are the market
u10l4-3.explanation: It's pure arithmetic: it doesn't depend on whether managers are good or bad.

u10l4-4.prompt: Funds that beat their index one year usually do it again in the following years.
u10l4-4.explanation: SPIVA also measures persistence: very few repeat. Past success doesn't predict the future.

u10l4-5.prompt: Imagine you're an active manager and your job is to call where the market is heading. This is a major stock index. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u10l4-5.explanation: Calling the market's next move again and again is what active management tries to do, and what almost nobody manages consistently.

u10l4-6.prompt: Bruno picks his fund from the league table: he buys last year's top performer, up +45 %. What would you tell him?
options: Good idea: if it rose that much, the manager is a genius
That last year's table barely predicts next year's, and he should look at costs and policy
To buy the top five in the table to be safe
u10l4-6.explanation: A fund's past returns say very little about future ones; costs, on the other hand, stay.
feedback: Very few repeat. Often the biggest riser in a year is the one that took the most risk.
Good: according to SPIVA, chasing last year's winner usually goes badly.
Five one-year winners aren't five ten-year winners.

u10l4-7.prompt: According to Sharpe, why does the average active investor get less than the market?
options: Because managers don't know how to invest
Because before costs they earn the same, and then they pay more costs
u10l4-7.explanation: It's the arithmetic of active management (Sharpe, 1991).

u10l4-8.prompt: An index fund tries to beat its index.
u10l4-8.explanation: It tries to copy it at the lowest possible cost.

u10l4-9.prompt: The report that compares active funds with their index is called ____.
u10l4-9.explanation: S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes it for Europe, the US and other regions.

u10l4-10.prompt: Which conclusions are reasonable from SPIVA? Select all.
options: Costs explain a large part of the gap
It's hard to know in advance who will beat the index
No active manager has ever beaten the market
Most active funds don't beat their index over the long run
u10l4-10.explanation: Some do beat it; the problem is that they're few and almost impossible to spot in advance.

u10l5-1.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u10l5-1.explanation: Accumulating and distributing only change what's done with the dividends and when they're taxed.
right: Pays the dividends to the unitholder
You don't pay until you sell
The 19 % taken off when you're paid

u10l5-2.prompt: A distributing ETF pays you €400 in dividends this year. With 19 % withheld, how much reaches you?
u10l5-2.explanation: 400 × 0.81 = €324. The other €76 go to Hacienda this year.

u10l5-3.prompt: In Spain, which version is usually more tax-efficient for building wealth over years?
u10l5-3.explanation: Since it doesn't pay out, you're not taxed on the dividends until you sell, and everything keeps compounding.

u10l5-4.prompt: Marta, already retired, wants to top up her pension with income every quarter. Pablo, 24, wants his money to grow for 30 years. Which version suits each of them?
u10l5-4.explanation: The right version depends on whether you need income now or want to grow your wealth.
feedback: Pablo would pay tax every year on dividends he doesn't need.
Good: Marta needs income; Pablo needs his money to compound without paying tax every year.
The other way round: Marta would have to sell units to get income and Pablo would pay tax for no reason.

u10l5-5.prompt: An accumulating ETF doesn't receive the dividends of the companies it holds.
u10l5-5.explanation: It does receive them, but it reinvests them inside the fund instead of paying them to you.

options: Useful for living off the income
You don't pay tax until you sell
You're taxed on the dividends every year
Pays money into your account every quarter
u10l5-6.explanation: Accumulating = reinvest and defer tax. Distributing = receive income that's taxed every year.

u10l5-7.prompt: You invest €10,000 in an accumulating fund that receives 3 % a year in dividends and reinvests them. Not counting price rises, how much would you have after 2 years? (round)

u10l5-8.prompt: Quick: which version pays you the dividends?
u10l5-8.explanation: The distributing one (Dist) pays them out; the accumulating one (Acc) reinvests them.

options: You earn the same, just reinvested, and in Spain you pay tax later
You're right, the accumulating one gives you nothing
The distributing one returns twice as much
u10l5-9.explanation: Both versions hold the same companies; what changes is when you get paid and when you're taxed.
feedback: That's it! Not seeing the money doesn't mean you're not earning it.
It does: the dividends are reinvested and your units are worth more.
Before tax they return the same; after tax, the distributing one usually lags a little if you don't need the income.
lines: I prefer the distributing one: that way I «see» the money 💸
With the accumulating one it feels like I'm not earning anything.

u10l5-10.prompt: What a distributing fund pays out is taxed in the year you ____ it.
u10l5-10.explanation: That's why, if you don't need that income, you pay tax earlier than you have to.

u10l6-1.prompt: What's true of a physically replicated ETF? Select all.
options: It may buy just a representative sample
It may lend out securities in exchange for a fee
It depends on a swap with a bank
It buys the shares in the index
u10l6-1.explanation: The swap belongs to synthetic replication.

u10l6-2.prompt: What are the features of synthetic replication? Select all.
options: Under UCITS, counterparty exposure is capped at 10 %
It doesn't track the index at all
u10l6-2.explanation: It tracks the index, often very precisely; its particular risk is the counterparty.

u10l6-3.prompt: In a synthetic ETF, who pays the index's return?
options: The swap counterparty, usually a bank
u10l6-3.explanation: The bank commits to paying whatever the index does in exchange for what the ETF's basket returns.

u10l6-4.prompt: A synthetic ETF holds no assets at all.
u10l6-4.explanation: It holds a basket of assets that serves as collateral; through the swap it receives the index's return.

u10l6-5.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u10l6-5.explanation: These are the pieces for understanding how an ETF copies its index and how precisely.
right: How far it strays from the index in a year
Buys every stock in the index

u10l6-6.prompt: An index rises 10.00 % in a year and the ETF that replicates it, 9.78 %. What is the tracking difference in points?
u10l6-6.explanation: 10.00 − 9.78 = 0.22 points, in line with what a cheap ETF costs.

u10l6-7.prompt: Ana is comparing two ETFs on the same index: a physical one with a TER of 0.07 % and a synthetic one with a TER of 0.05 %. What else does she look at?
options: The actual tracking difference, the ETF's size and its replication method
Which one has the shorter name
u10l6-7.explanation: Two ETFs on the same index can differ in real costs, size and replication risks.
feedback: Good: those are the pieces for comparing two ETFs on the same index.
The name doesn't tell you how it replicates or how far it strays.
The TER matters, but so does how far it actually strays from the index, and its size.

u10l6-8.prompt: Sampling replication is common for indices with thousands of stocks.
u10l6-8.explanation: Buying thousands of small stocks would be expensive; a well-chosen sample tracks the index almost as closely.

options: Signs a swap with a bank
Lends out securities from its portfolio
A bank pays it the index's return
Buys the shares in the index
u10l6-9.explanation: Physical holds what's in the index; synthetic receives its return through a contract.

u10l6-10.prompt: In a synthetic ETF, the bank it signs the swap with is called the ____.
u10l6-10.explanation: If the counterparty fails, the ETF can lose up to what it's owed, which UCITS caps at 10 %.
